title: safe-repairers.json
description: The suite's own allowlist of scripts and skills that may be named as a repair recommendation in finding text, skill prose, hook output, or a docstring under bin/, backend_suite/engine/, hooks/, commands/, or agents/. Exists because a repair recommendation has cost real data twice (issue #109 — audit_copy's title_case fix corrupted proper nouns; issue #116 — sync_mock_api.py deleted correct fixture data), both times because the recommending text could not tell the difference between 'this script is safe to point someone at' and 'this script can silently destroy something'. audit_safe_repairers.py enforces that every script or skill named as a fix is on this list; being on the list is not a rubber stamp — every entry has to attest to the two things that make a recommendation survivable (R1: it does not write without an explicit flag or already writes only a diff; R2: it has a demonstrated refusal on a constructed data-loss case), and the attestation is checked for substance, not just presence, by audit_safe_repairers.py's own EXEMPT-style review process. This file lives in the universal plugin (not a project's `.backend-suite/`) because the scripts it is attesting to ARE the plugin's own bin/ and engine/ — a consumer project extends the equivalent check for its own hooks.map.json fixHint/repair.command values via doctor.py instead, which is a different registry for a different author.

invocation.description: The EXACT text that must appear for this entry to apply — a bare script basename ('repair_tokens.py'), a script plus a specific flag ('generate_openapi.py --check'), or a skill slash-form ('/establish-brand-voice'). Keyed on the invocation rather than only the script, because the same script can be safe under one flag and destructive under another (generate_openapi.py --check never writes; generate_openapi.py with no flag does) — allowlisting the bare name would launder the unsafe form in under the safe one's attestation. A bare-script entry covers every invocation of that script; a flagged entry covers only that exact flag combination and nothing else naming the same script.

kind.description: 'script' for a bin/ or engine/ Python or shell entry point; 'skill' for a '/slash-name' recommendation to invoke a plugin skill.

r1.description: R1 attestation: how this invocation avoids writing destructively — 'emits a diff/patch and never touches the working tree', 'refuses to run without an explicit --write (or equivalent) flag', or '--check is report-only by construction; the un-flagged form is NOT this entry and is not allowlisted'. Must name the actual mechanism, not just assert safety — a one-word 'safe' is indistinguishable from an unreviewed rubber stamp and audit_safe_repairers.py's own review rejects entries that read like one.

r2.description: R2 attestation: the demonstrated refusal on a constructed data-loss case. Name the actual test that proves it — a --selftest flag, or (for a script with no such flag) the specific test file and test case(s) that plant a scenario where blind application would lose or corrupt data and assert the script refuses rather than applying it. An entry whose R2 field describes a capability refusal (missing config, unresolvable input) but not a DATA-LOSS refusal is weaker evidence and must say so explicitly rather than overstate it.

selftestCommand.description: Optional: the exact command audit_safe_repairers.py (or a human) can run to reproduce the R2 proof. Omitted only when no such command exists yet and r2 says why the mechanism (not a runnable command) is trusted instead — see the repair_tokens.py entry for a worked example of that gap being named rather than hidden.

reason.description: Why this entry is on the list at all — provenance, who reviewed it, or a pointer to the issue that established the attestation. Mirrors audit_skill_paths.py's EXEMPT convention: an entry nobody can see the reasoning for is how a real finding gets suppressed for years.
